title: Metal and everything else — Image Wiki
text:
Metal and everything else
  Metals have almost no colour of their own and show you the room instead; everything else gets its colour from underneath and reflects the light's own colour on top. This is the sharpest material test you can run on an image.

  
    Termconductors (metals) vs dielectrics (non-metals)
    Also calledmetalness, metallic vs non-metallic, conductor and insulator
    Not the same asshiny vs metal, grey vs metal, painted metal
    Read10 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensWhat you can see in the picturePainted metal is not metalThe three metals that tintCommon mistakesWhy this is a good fake-image tell
      
    
  

  Stand a chrome kettle and a white ceramic mug on the same table. Photograph both. Now cover the table with a black cloth and photograph them again. The mug barely changes. The kettle changes completely — it was full of the room, and now it is full of black cloth.
That is not a difference of shininess; a glazed mug can be very shiny. It is a difference of category, and it is the one material distinction worth learning properly. Graphics people call the two groups conductors and dielectrics, or in plain use: metals, and everything else. Scratchapixel says to remember those two words because you will meet them constantly (SRC-094); Pixar's RenderMan course splits its material teaching along the same line (SRC-092), and PBRT gives conductors and dielectrics separate chapters (SRC-090).
Why it happens
Go back to the two routes light can take at a surface, from Diffuse and specular: it goes in and comes back out coloured, or it bounces off the boundary keeping the light's own colour. Metal and non-metal differ in how the arriving light divides between them.

100% arriving60–90%reflectedthe little that gets in is absorbedMetal (conductor)gold, copper, steel, chrome, aluminiumno colour of its own — you see the room100% arriving0–20%reflectedthe rest goes in, is filtered, and comes back outNon-metal (dielectric)plastic, ceramic, stone, skin, water, paintits colour comes from inside

Band widths are to scale; the same 100% arrives in both panels.
Left, a conductor. Marmoset's figure is 60–90% straight back off the boundary (SRC-086). The thin remainder that gets in is absorbed rather than scattered, so nothing returns from inside — no body colour to fall back on. The ball below has nothing to be except its surroundings: a bright band where the ceiling is, a dark band where the floor is, two window shapes.
Right, a dielectric. Only 0–20% bounces off the boundary (SRC-086); Scratchapixel's number for the middle of a glass ball is around 6% (SRC-094). The rest goes in, is filtered by the pigment, and leaves again as diffuse body colour. That ball has a colour of its own, plus one small highlight in the colour of the light.
One caveat the drawing cannot show: only some conductors tint what they reflect. Gold, copper and brass do. Steel, chrome, silver, nickel and aluminium are near-neutral.




Conductor: a polished steel sphere outdoors
Dielectric: a glass ball held against the sky


Both figures by Scratchapixel, Reflection, Refraction and Fresnel, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source. Two spheres, the same problem, opposite answers — the band widths in the diagram above, photographed.
The steel sphere turns nearly everything back at its front face, so the front face is the whole picture: white sky along the top, a brick office block with pale columns and near-black windows across the middle, a dome at the right, paving slabs sweeping over the bottom, and the photographer standing in the middle of it. Follow the joints between the paving slabs — straight lines on the ground, bent into arcs on the ball. Nothing in it is steel-coloured: the brick comes back brick-red and the sky white.
The glass ball does the opposite with the same arriving light. A few per cent bounces off the boundary — the single sun glint near the top is most of it — and the rest goes in. What fills the ball is therefore the far side of the world, upside down: treetops hanging from the upper edge, the horizon line running across it, and the photographer's own fingertips showing through at the bottom.
Glass is the transparent extreme of the dielectric side, so nothing scatters inside it and it has no body colour of its own — that part it does not share with the porcelain and moss further down this page, whose pigment scatters what enters. The split at the boundary is the same either way: a few per cent off, the rest in.


Metals are opaque to light in a way non-metals are not (SRC-094): a conductor absorbs rather than scatters whatever does penetrate, so in theory it shows no diffuse light at all — in practice you get a little, from oxides and grime on the surface (SRC-086). So the reliable rule is a subtraction, not an addition:

Metal: no body colour. What you see is the environment, at high strength.
Everything else: body colour, plus a weak reflection in the colour of the light.

The tint is a bonus tell on top, and Marmoset is explicit that colouring is rare even among conductors (SRC-086). A gold-coloured highlight proves metal. A neutral one proves nothing either way.
What you can see in the picture



Mary Harrsch, Silver water jug by Obadiah Rich, Boston, 1845–1850, at the Portland Art Museum, 2012. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
Read the room off the jug. The olive-yellow gallery wall comes back as a warm band wrapped round the belly and neck; the dark band under it is the wood panelling; the pale wedge lower down is the plinth, and the fan-shaped streaks up on the shoulder are something overhead. Every value on this object is a value from somewhere else in the room.
Then notice what is not there: no silver-coloured shading, no lit side rolling smoothly into a dark side the way a ceramic jug would. Values jump from near-white to near-black within a centimetre, because neighbouring patches point at different things. And nothing is tinted — silver hands back the room's own colours, so the olive wall stays olive and the floor stays brown.


Give that same chrome sphere nothing to reflect and it comes back as a flat grey blob, because there is no diffuse colour underneath. Product photographers build reflection cards specifically to give metal something to be a picture of, and a generated image that puts metal in a featureless background usually gives itself away here. Brushed or machined metal scatters along the grain, which stretches highlights into streaks; PBRT names it as the extreme case of an anisotropic surface (SRC-091).


Metal: a silver teapot, c. 1795
Non-metal: a porcelain teapot, 1662–1722


Two teapots photographed by the same museum against the same plain grey backdrop under the same soft light. The only variable that matters is which of the two laws the surface obeys.
The silver pot has no colour. Its flat oval body is a broad pale sweep of the backdrop, mottled but featureless — nothing in that room to be a picture of. The curved parts give it away: the lid squeezes the whole studio into two centimetres, near-white on top then a hard dark line where the light stops, and the spout carries a razor-thin dark stripe along its ridge with a bright one below.
The porcelain pot keeps its own colours — white ground, iron-red flowers, green leaves — and holds their value round the form, brightening only where it turns toward the light. Its specular contribution is the small white glints on the shoulder and lid. Those are the light; the flowers are the pot.
Left: John A. Schanck, teapot, c. 1795. Right: Chinese, small covered wine pot or teapot, 1662–1722. Both Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0.


Painted metal is not metal
A car door is steel, but the surface light meets is clear-coated paint, and paint is a dielectric: coloured body, white highlight, a reflection of the sky in the clear coat. The chrome trim and the alloy wheel beside it are metal, environment-driven. Same car, two material laws, one frame. The same goes for anodised, powder-coated, enamelled, tarnished, greasy and dusty metal — whatever covers the metal is the surface. A rusted iron gate reads as rough coloured stone because iron oxide is a dielectric; only the bright worn edge where the coating is gone reads as metal.
The three metals that tint



R. Henrik Nilsson, Skultuna copper kettle, Skultuna, Sweden, presumably 1800s, 2024. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
The kettle does everything the silver jug did, with one addition. Follow the broad soft band down the right of the body: that is the bright sky, and it comes back copper-coloured, not white. The darker sweep across the left and lower body is the shaded ground, also coppery. Even at the base rim, where the surface points at the moss, the reflection turns a coppery green.
Compare the moss itself: green body colour held everywhere, a dull broad sheen instead of a mirror. A dielectric, and no amount of sunlight will make it show you the sky.






Metal (conductor)
Non-metal (dielectric)




Diffuse colour
essentially none
this is where its colour comes from


Colour of the reflection
tinted, but only for gold, copper and brass
the colour of the light


Amount reflected face-on
60–90%
0–20%


Put it in a black room
goes nearly black
keeps its colour, just unlit


Change the environment
appearance changes completely
shading changes, colour does not


Examples
gold, copper, brass, steel, aluminium, chrome
plastic, skin, wood, stone, water, paint, glass, cloth



Common mistakes

"Shiny means metal." A wet pebble, a glazed tile, a lacquered box and a soap bubble are all very shiny dielectrics. Shininess is roughness (Roughness and Fresnel), not metalness.
"Metal is grey." Steel, chrome, silver, nickel, platinum and aluminium are close to neutral, and their grey appearance is mostly the average of the room they are in. Gold, copper and brass are strongly coloured. Do not treat "grey" as the metal test.
"Dark metal is black metal." A metal that looks dark is usually reflecting something dark. Move the object, or move the light, and it stops being dark.
"Painted metal is metal." The paint is the surface. Judge the outermost layer, always.
"Something can be half metal." Not at a given point on the surface. A texture can mix metal and non-metal across an object — a scratched painted panel with bare aluminium showing through — but the physics at one spot is one or the other. A metalness slider is asking which of two laws to use, not for a blend of them.

Why this is a good fake-image tell
Generated images get metal wrong in three consistent ways, each of them one of the rules above, broken. Metal with a diffuse base colour: an object described as gold that renders as an even yellowish surface with a white highlight, evenly lit on all sides, no reflection of the room anywhere. That is yellow plastic. A reflection that matches no environment: smeared bright shapes on a kettle that do not resemble the window, the room or the photographer, and that do not stay consistent as the form curves — real reflections distort with the geometry in a way you can follow. A tint mismatch: silver-white highlights on gold, or gold-tinted highlights on plastic.

Metal or not, in five seconds

Find the brightest spot on the object. Is it the colour of the light in the scene, or the colour of the object? Object colour on a reflection means metal.
Can you read the environment in the surface — window shapes, a horizon, a dark floor band?
Is there a dark region as well as a bright one? Real metal usually has both.
Ask what the outermost layer actually is. Paint, rust, dust and grease all make it a dielectric.
If the object is supposedly metal but has an even body colour, no reflected environment, and a white highlight, you are looking at plastic pretending.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Diffuse and specular
              Light hitting a surface either goes in and comes back out coloured, or bounces straight off keeping the light's own colour. Almost everything a material looks like follows from the split between those two.
            
          
        
          
            
              Roughness and Fresnel
              Two dials that finish a material. Roughness decides how blurry the reflection is; Fresnel makes every surface more reflective at glancing angles. Between them they explain why real objects are never evenly shiny.
            
          
        
          
            
              Naming what is wrong
              A checklist for turning "something looks off" into a specific, defensible sentence about the image.
            
          
        
          
            
              The colour of the light
              What you see is the object's own colour multiplied by the light's colour — and your brain quietly divides the light back out, which is why a white shirt looks white everywhere.
